title: Strategies for Strengthening Social Integration and Promoting Self-Esteem Among Adolescents with Special Needs in Northern Namibia
authors: Linus Mupenda Shipena; Antony Chege; Lornah Irene Ayako
abstract: In northern Namibia, adolescents with special needs face developmental challenges of adolescence in addition to the stigma associated with disabilities due to local cultural beliefs. This highlights an urgent yet under-explored need for context-specific strategies to enhance their social integration and self-esteem. Current Namibian studies on disability and inclusive education have concentrated primarily on recording policy and implementation deficiencies, resulting in a lack of empirically based, locally developed approaches to enhance the psychosocial welfare of this group. This study addressed that gap by establishing strategies for strengthening social integration and promoting self-esteem among adolescents with special needs in northern Namibia. The study was guided by Social Identity Theory and Rogers’ Self-Concept Theory and adopted a convergent parallel mixed-methods design. Quantitative data were collected from 192 adolescents with special needs using the Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support and the Robson Self-Concept Questionnaire. Qualitative data, which formed the primary basis for this objective, were drawn from semi-structured interviews with six purposively selected participants and analysed using thematic content analysis. Four strategy-oriented themes emerged: strengthening support systems around family, teachers and hostel matrons; expanding co-curricular activities and social opportunities; improving inclusive learning environments through adaptive teaching and specialised materials; and promoting self-acceptance and disability awareness through structured sensitisation and mentorship. These themes closely matched the quantitative results, especially the relatively lower scores noted for trust in peer relationships and for self-worth items reflecting vulnerability (indicative of low self-esteem), suggesting that participants’ recommendations addressed real, assessable deficiencies instead of vague desires. The study concludes that a coordinated, multi-level strategy, combining consistent family and teacher support, structured peer and co-curricular opportunities, inclusive classroom practice and deliberate disability-awareness programming, offers the most promising route to strengthening social integration and self-esteem in this setting. Schools, families and policymakers are encouraged to adopt this coordinated approach, and future research should evaluate the effectiveness of interventions built on these strategies using pre-post or longitudinal designs.
venue: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science

rawPayload.snippet: In northern Namibia, adolescents with special needs face developmental challenges of adolescence in addition to the stigma associated with disabilities due to local cultural beliefs. This highlights an urgent yet under-explored need for context-specific strategies to enhance their social integration

rawPayload.venue: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science
